His past medical history is significant for celiac disease, for which he eats a gluten-free diet. He reports that he stepped on a nail last week, but the nail did not seem rusty so he just washed his feet afterward. His wife reports that he has been up to date on his tetanus vaccinations. Physical examination demonstrates weakness and fasciculations of the left upper extremity along with spastic clonus of the left ankle. The patient denies gait disturbances, vision or hearing changes, headaches, nausea/vomiting, gastrointestinal disturbances, or incontinence. What is best next step in terms of management for this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 56-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife for complaints of progressive weakness for the past 3 months. He reports difficulty eating, especially when chewing foods like steak. The wife complains that he has been “out of it lately and has been forgetting my birthday." His past medical history is significant for celiac disease, for which he eats a gluten-free diet. He reports that he stepped on a nail last week, but the nail did not seem rusty so he just washed his feet afterward. His wife reports that he has been up to date on his tetanus vaccinations. Physical examination demonstrates weakness and fasciculations of the left upper extremity along with spastic clonus of the left ankle. The patient denies gait disturbances, vision or hearing changes, headaches, nausea/vomiting, gastrointestinal disturbances, or incontinence. What is best next step in terms of management for this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Donepezil
opb. Levodopa
opc. Riluzole
opd. Tetanus immunoglobulin and vaccine
ope. Vitamin B12

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with progressive weakness, difficulty chewing, and cognitive changes, which suggest a possible neurological disorder. The examination reveals weakness and fasciculations in the left upper extremity and spastic clonus of the left ankle, indicating a potential motor neuron disease. Riluzole is indicated for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and other motor neuron diseases, aligning with the symptoms observed. While vitamin B12 deficiency could explain some neurological symptoms, the specific presentation of weakness and fasciculations is more consistent with a motor neuron disease, making Riluzole the most appropriate next step. The patient's celiac disease raises concern for malabsorption, but he is not exhibiting classic signs of vitamin B12 deficiency. Tetanus immunoglobulin is unnecessary as the patient is up to date on vaccinations, and Donepezil is not indicated given the primary neurological symptoms. Therefore, the best next step in management is Riluzole.
